\chapter{What It Costs}
\label{ch:ml-shopping}
\hlchaptermodality{91}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can go into a shop, ask what something costs, understand the answer and say that I am buying it.}

From cold: the shop, the price, the money, the rupee and the buying verb, run as a four-line scene, and an accounting of how much of that scene was already owned.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[kaṭa]{\ml{കട} (kaṭa) — a shop}

\label{lesson:ML-C91-kada}



\begin{quote}
Say the ending that means \textbf{in} or \textbf{at}, the one you have had since the first verbs.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{കട}}
\textbf{\ml{കട}} — \emph{kaṭa} — a shop.

This book has taught you rice, water, tea, coffee, milk, salt and a knife, and \textbf{not one word for the place any of them comes from.} That is the hole this chapter is here to fill, and it starts with the building.

It takes the in-ending exactly as you would expect, joining with a \textbf{-\ml{യ}-} because the word ends in \textbf{\ml{അ}}:

\textbf{\ml{കടയിൽ}} — \emph{kaṭayil} — in the shop, at the shop.

Nothing about that join is new. \textbf{It is the same choice the owner-ending makes}, decided by the same thing — the last sound of the noun.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kaṭa}
  \item \emph{kaṭayil}
  \item what decided the \textbf{-\ml{യ}-} in the middle
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is a \emph{kaṭa}? (\textbf{A shop}.) How do you say \emph{at the shop}? (\emph{\textbf{kaṭayil}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vila paṇaṁ]{\ml{വില} \ml{പണം} (vila, paṇaṁ) — price and money}

\label{lesson:ML-C91-vila-panam}



\begin{quote}
Say the word for a shop, and say it again meaning \emph{at the shop}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{വില}, \ml{പണം}}
\textbf{\ml{വില}} — \emph{vila} — price, cost.

\textbf{\ml{പണം}} — \emph{paṇaṁ} — money.

Two words, and between them they open a whole situation the book has kept shut.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{വില}} & what a thing \textbf{costs} \\
\textbf{\ml{പണം}} & what you \textbf{pay with} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

English keeps them apart the same way, so there is nothing to untangle.

\textbf{\ml{പണം} ends in the \ml{ം}}, which means you already know what it will do when a case ending attaches to it: the \textbf{\ml{ം}} gives way, exactly as it did on the state name and on the book. A word that ends this way tells you in advance how it will behave.

\textbf{\ml{പുസ്തകത്തിന്റെ} \ml{വില}} — \emph{pustakattinṟe vila} — the price of the book.

Read that and every piece is old but one. \textbf{\ml{പുസ്തകം}} changed shape before its ending, took the owner-ending, and \textbf{\ml{വില}} followed it — the arrangement the place-words chapter established, carrying a new word.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{vila}
  \item \emph{paṇaṁ}
  \item which of the two is what a thing costs
  \item \emph{pustakattinṟe vila}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{vila}? (\textbf{Price}.) What is \emph{paṇaṁ}? (\textbf{Money}.) And what does the \textbf{\ml{ം}} on the second one warn you about? (\textbf{It will give way when a case ending attaches}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ethra rūpa]{\ml{എത്ര} \ml{രൂപ} (ethra rūpa) — how many rupees?}

\label{lesson:ML-C91-ethra-rupa}



\begin{quote}
Say the word that asks \textbf{how much}. Then count the tens from thirty as far as you can.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{രൂപ}, and the question it answers}
\textbf{\ml{രൂപ}} — \emph{rūpa} — a rupee.

And now the question the whole chapter has been aiming at:

\textbf{\ml{എത്ര} \ml{രൂപ}?} — \emph{ethra rūpa?} — \textbf{how many rupees?} What does it cost?

\textbf{Look at what that cost you.} \textbf{\ml{എത്ര}} was lifted out of the age question two chapters after you first met it, and it has been yours since. \textbf{\ml{രൂപ}} is the one new word on this page. \textbf{The question is two words and one of them is old.}

The answer was out of reach until very recently:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{അമ്പത്} \ml{രൂപ}} & fifty rupees \\
\textbf{\ml{നൂറ്} \ml{രൂപ}} & a hundred rupees \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{Before the counting chapter you could not have said either.} The count stopped at twenty, so every price above it was unsayable — which is exactly what that chapter's exam point warned about.

So this page is where three separate chapters meet: \textbf{the word that asks, the numbers that answer, and the unit they are counted in.}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{rūpa}
  \item \emph{ethra rūpa?}
  \item \emph{ampathŭ rūpa}
  \item \emph{nūṟŭ rūpa}
  \item which word in the question you already owned
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you ask a price? (\emph{\textbf{ethra rūpa?}}) How many words is that? (\textbf{Two}.) And how many of them were new today? (\textbf{One}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vāṅṅuka]{\ml{വാങ്ങുക} (vāṅṅuka) — to buy}

\label{lesson:ML-C91-vaanguka}



\begin{quote}
Ask a price. Then say the verb \emph{to take}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{വാങ്ങുക}}
\textbf{\ml{വാങ്ങുക}} — \emph{vāṅṅuka} — to buy.

It is built the way your verbs are built, on the \textbf{-\ml{ഉക}} ending you have had since your first ones, so there is nothing new in its shape — only its meaning.

\textbf{\ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{പുസ്തകം} \ml{വാങ്ങുന്നു}} — \emph{ñān pustakaṁ vāṅṅunnu} — I buy the book.

Look at the object. \textbf{\ml{പുസ്തകം}} is bare — \textbf{no ending on it} — because it is a thing and not a person, which is the rule the object chapter gave you. The verb changed and the rule did not.

With this word the chapter closes a circle. \textbf{You can name the place, ask the price, hear a number back, and say what you are doing there} — and of those four, only the place, the price and this verb were new.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{vāṅṅuka}
  \item \emph{ñān pustakaṁ vāṅṅunnu}
  \item why the book carries no ending
  \item \emph{kaṭayil}, then the whole sentence again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{vāṅṅuka}? (\textbf{To buy}.) Which ending does it share with your other verbs? (\textbf{-\ml{ഉക}}.) And does the thing you buy take an object ending? (\textbf{No — it is not a person}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vila enna ōrmma]{(what it costs) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ML-R91-shopping-recall}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say \emph{shop}, \emph{price} and \emph{money}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange — a whole scene, in five words}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{കട}} & a shop \\
\textbf{\ml{വില}} & price \\
\textbf{\ml{പണം}} & money \\
\textbf{\ml{രൂപ}} & a rupee \\
\textbf{\ml{വാങ്ങുക}} & to buy \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Put them in the order the situation happens in:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{കടയിൽ}} — at the shop.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{എത്ര} \ml{രൂപ}?} — how many rupees?
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{അമ്പത്} \ml{രൂപ}.} — fifty rupees.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{പുസ്തകം} \ml{വാങ്ങുന്നു}.} — I buy the book.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A scene, and most of it was already paid for.

\textbf{Count what was actually new on those four lines.} The shop, the rupee, the buying verb — \textbf{three words.} Everything else arrived earlier and was waiting:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{piece} & \textbf{where it came from} \\
\midrule
\textbf{-\ml{ഇൽ}} on the shop & your first verbs \\
\textbf{\ml{എത്ര}} & lifted out of the age question \\
\textbf{\ml{അമ്പത്}} & the counting chapter \\
\textbf{\ml{പുസ്തകം}} bare, with no object ending & the object chapter's rule for things \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{The numbers matter most here.} Before the count went past twenty, every price above it was unsayable — which is exactly what that chapter's exam point had warned. \textbf{Teaching the tens is what made a price answerable}, and this chapter only had to name what is being counted.

That is worth noticing about the shape of the work: \textbf{a vocabulary chapter is cheap when the grammar under it has already been built}, and expensive when it has not.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kaṭayil}
  \item \emph{ethra rūpa?}
  \item a price of your own, using any ten you know
  \item \emph{ñān pustakaṁ vāṅṅunnu}
  \item which three words on this page were new
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you ask what something costs? (\emph{\textbf{ethra rūpa?}}) What is \emph{vila}? (\textbf{Price}.) And what had to be taught before a price could be answered at all? (\textbf{The numbers past twenty}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
